data.headword: ntəšle/notəš i qundaraye di kalo 'der Braut den Schuh wegschnappen (Hochzeitsbrauch)'
data.turoyo: Kətwo ʕade nətšiwo. U ḥa d nutašwo w mahzamwo i qundaraye di kalo w d mawbela l su ḥaṯno gəd ubele kallat.
data.translation: There was a custom: they used to snatch them. Whoever snatched and carried off the bride's shoe and brought it to the bridegroom, he would give him a little money.

rationale: Conventional wedding collocation followed by a gift, confirmed by /1682–1685. Searches qundar and ntošo returned no existing listing. Supplied English is machine translation.

summary: All 25 supplied occurrences fit the same snatching/tearing/abduction meaning; human and inanimate patients do not require separate senses.
L-marked nominal agents occur with Preterit suffixal agents (children, fox, mother); zero-marked patients and m-source phrases coexist. Infectum patients can be overt NPs or suffixes.

The sole existing Preterit, Infectum and Infectum-wa examples are unnumbered in the parsed entry; explicit sense assignments repair the structure. Existing Detransitive Preterit is also unnumbered, with no sense list; its counterpart is now stated as Detransitive 1.

21/2 and 66/288 already occur in the entry. Repeated bride-abduction reports at 67/144 and /156 are already cited; other near-identical reports do not crowd out distinct food, tearing and source-complement contexts.
Ko disa ntəšle at 67/239 does not securely prove ko-Preterit: a presentative ko followed by an ordinary Preterit is possible. No new ko-Preterit box is published.
Ntošano is an article-governed action nominal; Infinitiv is supported directly. Nothing here motivates a separate snatching-collocation list.
Round 2 only. Jan English is a project machine translation; semantic decisions are based on the Turoyo. Round-1 proposals remain prior material and are not re-proposed here.
Habitual nətšiwo/nutašwo contrasts with Preterit ntəšše and Preterit-wa ntəšwolle. The latter has the L-agent series; nətšiwola/nutašwola instead carry a feminine patient.
A bride-shoe collocation is established by an explicit custom and payment description. It belongs in Idiomatic phrases while literal snatching remains I.1.
The self-correction at 1.38/1685 prevents treating the initial own-shoe assertion as an unqualified event report. The clear bride-shoe clause is quoted instead.
67/239: is separated ko before disa a verbal preverb or an independent presentative? Confirm before adding ko-Preterit.
67/195: confirm exact segmentation of contracted notašna; 67/131: does -ayḏe in quoted nxiraytayḏe reflect narrative perspective?
92/25: identify the antecedent of the second u zʕuro; the rescue discourse suggests the attacking snake targets the rescuer.
The inherited head questions the MEA etymology; corpus evidence here does not resolve it.
At Jan 1.38/1685, is the initial own-shoe assertion a false start or a shift in reference before the later denial?
Confirm number and suffix segmentation of ntəšwolle and singular nutašwola, preserving the printed variants.
At Jan 1.38/1682, are cushions another object of the same wedding custom or a separate practice?
Jan confirms the round-1 Infinitiv and source construction. Snatching wedding shoes is a culturally conventional collocation, not an additional verb sense.
